passage:
Monday: Kalyani, twelve, had a history project due on Friday. She watched cartoons instead. "Tomorrow," she said.
Wednesday: Nothing done. Her friend Arohi offered her own finished project to copy. "Just change the colours." Kalyani's stomach twisted. She wanted to say yes. She said, "No. I'll do mine," and stayed up late drawing a messy map.
The next week: She got a C and a comment: "Rushed but honest." That Sunday she stuck a small timetable above her desk: thirty minutes each evening, cartoons after. For the next project she started on day one.

qa.q: What did Arohi offer Kalyani?
qa.a: Her own finished project to copy.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani's stomach twist when Arohi made the offer?
qa.a: She was tempted because she was behind, but she felt that copying would be wrong.

qa.q: What change did Kalyani make, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: A small daily timetable with cartoons after work, which stops the last-minute rush.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Kalyani says no?
qa.a: Perhaps a little surprised or awkward about offering, but she may respect Kalyani's choice.

grounding: It shows a girl moving from procrastination through a cheating temptation to an honest study routine.

passage: Omkar, you want to hear about the exam hall? When I was twelve, a boy passed me a chit with the maths answers and whispered, "Irfan, take it." The invigilator was looking out of the window. My heart was banging. I hadn't studied much; I'd played marbles all week. I pushed the chit back without opening it. I got 41 out of 100, and my father was quiet for a whole day. But that night I made a rule for myself: one hour of study before marbles, every day. The next year I got 78. And I never had to wonder whether the marks were really mine.

qa.q: What did young Irfan score in that maths exam?
qa.a: 41 out of 100.

qa.q: What was young Irfan feeling in the moment the heart started banging?
qa.a: Irfan was scared and tempted, knowing Irfan hadn't studied and that using the chit would be cheating.

qa.q: Which choice in the exam hall turned out to matter most, and why?
qa.a: Pushing the chit back unopened; the low mark hurt, but it led to Irfan's daily study rule and marks that were truly Irfan's own.

qa.q: How might Irfan's father have felt about the 41 out of 100?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed, since he stayed quiet for a whole day, though he did not know Irfan had refused to cheat.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a child refusing to cheat after slacking and then building a steady study habit.

passage: It was exam week, and the house next door was hosting a wedding: drums until midnight, lights flashing through the window. Parul, eleven, kept to her plan anyway: up at six when it was quiet, revise for an hour, reach school on time. Her cousin Ankita, visiting for the wedding, begged, "Come to the mehendi, just skip tonight's revision." Parul looked at her timetable. "I'll come after I finish chapter four." She stuffed cotton wool in her ears, finished by nine, then went and danced for an hour. The next morning she was still at the bus stop by seven.

qa.q: What time did Parul get up to revise?
qa.a: At six, when it was quiet.

qa.q: Why did Parul look at her timetable before answering Ankita?
qa.a: She felt torn between joining the fun and sticking to her plan, so she checked how she could do both.

qa.q: Which of Parul's choices shows a good balance?
qa.a: Finishing chapter four before joining the celebration let her keep her routine and still enjoy the wedding.

qa.q: How might Ankita see Parul's choice?
qa.a: She may think Parul is too strict, but she gets her cousin at the mehendi in the end.

grounding: It shows a girl keeping a diligent, punctual study routine despite a noisy wedding and a tempting invitation.

passage: At 7:40, in the lobby of their building in Pune, Devika held out her maths notebook. 'Just copy the last four. The bus comes in ten minutes.' Yogesh looked at the neat columns. He had left the sums for last night and then watched cartoons till dinner. His fingers actually touched the notebook. Then he pushed it back. 'Ma'am will call me to do one on the board, and I'll stand there like a statue.' He sat on the steps and did two sums fast and messily, and wrote 'will finish at lunch' beside the rest. On the bus he muttered, 'Tonight, sums before cartoons.' Devika shrugged, but she put her notebook back in her bag.

qa.q: What time was it when Devika offered her notebook?
qa.a: It was 7:40.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh push the notebook back after touching it?
qa.a: He was tempted, but he worried about being asked to solve a sum on the board, and he seemed to know copying would not fix his delay.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do so this morning rush does not happen again?
qa.a: He could stick to his own plan of sums before cartoons, doing homework soon after school.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when he refused?
qa.a: She may have felt a little brushed off, but her shrug and putting the notebook away suggest she accepted it.

grounding: Shows a child tempted to copy after putting off homework, choosing honest partial work and a new routine.

passage:
'Pooja, isn't the volcano model due Monday?'
'Papa, it's only Friday.'
'And tomorrow is Nani's birthday lunch. And Sunday you have dance.'
'...Oh.'
'So when were you planning to build it?'
'I thought Wasim was doing most of it.'
'Is that what Wasim thinks?'
Pooja picked at the sofa cushion. 'He did the drawing last week. I said I'd do the clay.'
'Then the clay is yours.'
'Can't you just make it tonight? You're good at this.'
'I'll sit with you. Your hands, though, not mine.'
She groaned, then went to find the clay. 'Fine. But you hold the bottle when we test it.'
'Deal. Call Wasim first and tell him honestly where it stands.'

qa.q: When is the volcano model due?
qa.a: It is due on Monday.

qa.q: What does Pooja picking at the cushion suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She likely felt a bit guilty as she realised she had not done her share of the project.

qa.q: How did Papa support her without doing the work for her?
qa.a: He helped her see how little time was left and offered to sit with her, but insisted on her own hands and on being honest with Wasim.

qa.q: If you were Wasim, what would you want from Pooja?
qa.a: I would want her to do the clay she promised and tell me honestly if she was behind, so Monday is not a surprise.

grounding: Shows a child's procrastination on a shared project and a parent steering her toward doing her own part honestly.
